title: Every Spiritual Blessing
subtitle: Ephesians 1:1–14
description: Paul opens his letter to Ephesus with one long sentence of praise for every blessing given in Christ.
paragraphs: The letter comes from a man in chains to the city where he had lived and taught longer than almost anywhere else. Acts tells how Paul spent the better part of three years in Ephesus, and how the elders of its church later met him on the beach at Miletus and wept, knowing they would not see his face again. Now a letter travels back to that church from his imprisonment. It opens the way his letters open, with his own name and theirs: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God,” writing “To the saints in Ephesus, the faithful in Christ Jesus.” Then the greeting he never seems to tire of: “Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

What follows is not a request, a warning, or a piece of news. It is one long sentence of praise, and Paul lets it run. “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms.” The blessing starts before their story starts. “For He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in His presence.” And it reaches forward as well as back: “In love He predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of His will,” all of it “to the praise of His glorious grace, which He has freely given us in the Beloved One.”

Inside that grace stands a rescue with a price on it. “In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of His grace”, a grace “that He lavished on us with all wisdom and understanding.” And with the rescue comes a secret brought out into the open. “And He has made known to us the mystery of His will according to His good pleasure, which He purposed in Christ,” a plan “to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ.”

The choosing has a purpose, and Paul states it plainly. “In Him we were also chosen as God’s own, having been predestined according to the plan of Him who works out everything by the counsel of His will,” and this was “in order that we, who were the first to hope in Christ, would be for the praise of His glory.”

Then the sentence turns from we to you, and the blessing lands in Ephesus itself. Having heard and believed “the word of truth,” the gospel of their salvation, they “were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.” The seal is not the end of the matter but a pledge toward it: the Spirit is the one “who is the pledge of our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God’s possession, to the praise of His glory.” The long sentence that began with God blessing His people ends where it kept landing all along, on the praise of His glory.

title: Eyes of the Heart Enlightened
subtitle: Ephesians 1:15–23
description: Paul reports his prayer for the Ephesian believers, that the eyes of their hearts would be opened.
paragraphs: The blessing is barely finished before Paul is on his knees, and he tells them why. “For this reason, ever since I heard about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints, I have not stopped giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers.” A prisoner who cannot go to them does the one thing his chains cannot stop. He prays for them by name, and he reports the prayer so they can hear what he asks God for on their behalf.

He does not ask for their circumstances to change. He asks for their sight to change. He prays “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glorious Father, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in your knowledge of Him.” Then comes the image at the center of the prayer: “I ask that the eyes of your heart may be enlightened, so that you may know the hope of His calling, the riches of His glorious inheritance in the saints.” Hearts, in Paul's telling, have eyes, and eyes can be opened. What he wants them to see is hope with a source, the calling God gave, and an inheritance he calls glorious and rich.

And one more sight beyond those: “the surpassing greatness of His power to us who believe.” This power is not a theory to Paul. He points to where it was last seen at full strength: the strength “which He exerted in Christ when He raised Him from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly realms.” The man writing from custody measures God's power by a resurrection and a throne.

From that throne the prayer opens out to the whole order of things. Christ sits “far above all rule and authority, power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in the present age but also in the one to come.” Every rival title, in this age and the next, is under Him. “And God put everything under His feet and made Him head over everything for the church.”

The letter's first prayer ends by bringing that cosmic headship home to the people hearing it. The church, this gathering of believers in Ephesus and far beyond it, is “His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all.” The One who fills everything is somehow fully present in this body of ordinary people, and Paul will spend the rest of the letter showing what that means.

title: Made Alive Together
subtitle: Ephesians 2:1–10
description: Dead in trespasses and made alive with Christ; salvation by grace through faith.
paragraphs: Paul turns from what God is like to what his readers were like, and he does not soften it. “And you were dead in your trespasses and sins,” dead “in which you used to walk when you conformed to the ways of this world and of the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit who is now at work in the sons of disobedience.” Then he widens the charge to include himself and everyone: “All of us also lived among them at one time, fulfilling the cravings of our flesh and indulging its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature children of wrath.” No one in the letter's audience gets to stand outside that sentence, least of all its author.

The turn of the whole passage is two words long: but God. “But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses.” The dead did not revive themselves. The same power that raised Christ reached people who could do nothing, and Paul interrupts his own sentence to announce the means of it: “It is by grace you have been saved!”

The rescue does not stop at survival. “And God raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus,” and Paul gives the reason, a display meant to run for ages: “in order that in the coming ages He might display the surpassing riches of His grace, demonstrated by His kindness to us in Christ Jesus.” The people God saved become the evidence of what His grace is like.

Then the letter's most famous sentence, stated with care so no one can mishear it: “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast.” Gift, not wages. Faith receives; it does not earn.

Works do come, but in their proper place, after the gift and because of it. “For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life.” The saved are God's own making, and the good they do was prepared for them like a road laid down before they ever walked it.

title: One New Humanity
subtitle: Ephesians 2:11–22
description: Gentiles who were far away are brought near and built into God’s household.
paragraphs: Now Paul turns and speaks directly to the Gentile believers, the ones who came to God from outside Israel, and his first word to them is remember. “Therefore remember that formerly you who are Gentiles in the flesh and called uncircumcised by the so-called circumcision”. He lists what their position had been, item by item, and none of it is flattering: “at that time you were separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise, without hope and without God in the world.” Separate, alienated, strangers, no hope, no God. That was the address of everyone in the room who was not born a Jew.

Then the same two-word turn as before, wearing different clothes: but now. “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ.” Distance was their condition; nearness is their new one, and it was bought, not earned.

The peace that made it possible has a name and a body. “For He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility.” Jew and Gentile were two peoples with a wall between them, and Christ “abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees” did it, Paul says, “to create in Himself one new man out of the two, thus making peace and reconciling both of them to God in one body through the cross.” One new humanity, not two peoples tolerating each other, and the cross is where the hostility died.

He carried the announcement himself: “He came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near. For through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit.” Both, one door, one Spirit. The far and the near arrive by the same road.

So Paul closes the account of what they were with what they are. “Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.” Strangers become citizens; foreigners become family. And the household has architecture: it is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone.” In Him “the whole building is fitted together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord,” and the last line lands on the Ephesian believers themselves: “in Him you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit.” The people who once had no God in the world are now the place where God dwells.

title: The Mystery Made Known
subtitle: Ephesians 3:1–13
description: Paul breaks off a prayer to explain the mystery: the Gentiles are fellow heirs in Christ.
paragraphs: Paul starts a sentence he will not finish for thirteen verses. “For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles”, and there it stops, mid-air, the way it stops in the letter itself. The prayer he was about to pray breaks off, and he turns aside to explain the thing his whole imprisonment is about. The sentence will wait at the side of the road until verse 14; what fills the gap is the mystery.

He calls it “the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, that is, the mystery made known to me by revelation.” The mystery of Christ, he says, was “not made known to men in other generations as it has now been revealed by the Spirit to God’s holy apostles and prophets.” Hidden for ages, and now read aloud in a letter by a prisoner. Anyone reading it, he says, can understand his insight into it.

Then he states it in one sentence, the center of the letter: “This mystery is that through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus.” Fellow heirs, not guests. Fellow members, not observers. The people who were strangers to the covenants of the promise are now partakers of the promise itself, on equal footing, through the gospel.

The steward of this news describes himself in the lowest terms available to him. “I became a servant of this gospel by the gift of God’s grace, given me through the working of His power.” And then: “Though I am less than the least of all the saints, this grace was given me: to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.” The least of the least, carrying riches he calls unsearchable to the very people the mystery concerns.

The audience for this unveiling turns out to be larger than the church. God kept the mystery hidden, Paul says, “that now, through the church, the manifold wisdom of God should be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms, according to the eternal purpose that He accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord.” The church, Jew and Gentile together in one body, is the display. Heaven itself learns what God was doing by looking at them. And the letter's readers get the practical end of it: “In Him and through faith in Him we may enter God’s presence with boldness and confidence.” So the prisoner asks them not to lose heart over the chains that brought them this letter: his sufferings for them, he says, are their glory. Then he goes back to the prayer he left waiting.

title: Rooted and Grounded in Love
subtitle: Ephesians 3:14–21
description: The prayer resumes, asking for strength and for power to grasp the size of Christ’s love.
paragraphs: Thirteen verses after he broke off, Paul comes back to the prayer, and he picks it up at the exact words where he left it. For this reason, he says, “I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name.” Every family, in heaven and on earth, named from one Father. The prisoner is on his knees, and the prayer he now prays is for the inner life of the people he cannot visit.

What he asks first is strength, but of a particular kind: “that out of the riches of His glory He may strengthen you with power through His Spirit in your inner being.” Power, but inward. And the purpose follows immediately: “so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith.” Not Christ visiting, but Christ dwelling, at home in their hearts through faith.

Then the prayer asks for power of a second kind, the power to take hold of love's size. Held there, “rooted and grounded in love”, they “will have power, together with all the saints, to comprehend the length and width and height and depth of the love of Christ, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge.” Paul asks them to know a love he says in the same breath surpasses knowledge, and he asks it not for a few of them but for all the saints together, as if no one believer is wide enough to measure it alone.

The end of the request is fullness itself: “that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.” It is the largest ask in the letter so far, and Paul makes it for people he describes as saints in a city he cannot enter, from a cell he cannot leave.

His answer to his own audacity is a hymn. “Now to Him who is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, according to His power that is at work within us, to Him be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.” The God who does more than the prayer can ask gets the glory, in the church and in Christ, for every generation coming. The first half of the letter, all blessing and mystery and prayer, closes there.

title: Walk Worthy of the Calling
subtitle: Ephesians 4:1–16
description: The letter turns from praise to the walk: unity, gifts, and a body growing into its head.
paragraphs: Here the letter turns. Half of Ephesians has been blessing, mystery, and prayer; the other half begins with a walk. “As a prisoner in the Lord, then, I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received.” The walk comes first in manners, not achievements: “with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, and with diligence to preserve the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace.” Unity, in Paul's handling, is not something they manufacture. It is something already given, and their work is to preserve it.

Because underneath the manners stands a row of ones. “There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to one hope when you were called; one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.” Seven ones, and the last of them holds all the others up.

One body does not mean one gift. “Now to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ.” Paul reaches for a psalm to say where the gifts came from: “When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men.” The ascended Christ is a giver, and what He gave the church was people: “it was He who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers, to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ.”

The gifts have a destination: “until we all reach unity in the faith and in the knowledge of the Son of God, as we mature to the full measure of the stature of Christ.” Maturity is the goal, and its opposite is a child in the water: “we will no longer be infants, tossed about by the waves and carried around by every wind of teaching and by the clever cunning of men in their deceitful scheming.”

Growth, when it comes, looks like this: “speaking the truth in love, we will in all things grow up into Christ Himself, who is the head.” The head supplies the body, and the body does its own growing: “From Him the whole body, fitted and held together by every supporting ligament, grows and builds itself up in love through the work of each individual part.” Each part working, the whole body building itself up in love. That is the picture of a church Paul is asking Ephesus to become.

title: The Old Self and the New
subtitle: Ephesians 4:17–32
description: The old self put off and the new self put on, worked out in speech, anger, work, and forgiveness.
paragraphs: Paul insists on the next thing with unusual weight: “So I tell you this, and insist on it in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their thinking.” He describes that old walk from the inside out: “They are darkened in their understanding and alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them due to the hardness of their hearts.” And the end of that road: “Having lost all sense of shame, they have given themselves over to sensuality for the practice of every kind of impurity, with a craving for more.”

His readers are not on that road, and he tells them why in the language of a classroom. “But this is not the way you came to know Christ. Surely you heard of Him and were taught in Him.” What they were taught comes in the grammar of clothing: “to put off your former way of life, your old self, which is being corrupted by its deceitful desires; to be renewed in the spirit of your minds; and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.” An old self taken off, a new self put on, and a mind renewed in between.

Then the teaching gets specific, one habit at a time. First the tongue: “Therefore each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to his neighbor, for we are all members of one another.” Then anger, with the words of a psalm standing inside his sentence: “Be angry, yet do not sin.” Anger has a curfew: “Do not let the sun set upon your anger, and do not give the devil a foothold.”

The thief's hands get a new trade: “He who has been stealing must steal no longer, but must work, doing good with his own hands, that he may have something to share with the one in need.” Speech gets the same treatment: “Let no unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building up the one in need and bringing grace to those who listen.” And underneath all of it, a warning about a Person: “do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.”

The passage ends with two lists facing each other. On one side: “Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger, outcry and slander, along with every form of malice.” On the other: “Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you.” The measure of their forgiving is the forgiving they received. That is the new self, described at street level.

title: Walk in Love, Light, and Wisdom
subtitle: Ephesians 5:1–21
description: Walking in love, as children of light, and in wisdom, filled with the Spirit.
paragraphs: The new chapter opens with the largest imitation ever asked of anyone: “Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God.” Children copy a father. The walk of love has a shape, and the shape is a man giving Himself up.

Against that walk Paul sets the old country's habits and bars them even from conversation: “among you, as is proper among the saints, there must not be even a hint of sexual immorality, or of any kind of impurity, or of greed.” In their place, thanksgiving. And he is blunt about the stakes: “of this you can be sure: No immoral, impure, or greedy person (that is, an idolater) has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.” No one is to talk them out of it: “Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of such things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.”

The reason is an identity, not a rule. “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light.” Not merely in the light, but light itself, and light has fruit: “the fruit of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth.” So they are to have “no fellowship with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them,” and over the whole passage stands an old saying Paul quotes without naming its source: “Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.”

The walk is also a walk in wisdom, and wisdom here is mostly about time: “Pay careful attention, then, to how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” And about what fills a person. “Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit.” The filling shows itself out loud: “Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Sing and make music in your hearts to the Lord, always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
The passage lands on a hinge the next one will swing on: “Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.” Everything Paul is about to say about households stands under that sentence.

title: Christ and the Church, at Home
subtitle: Ephesians 5:22–6:9
description: The teaching goes indoors: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters.
paragraphs: The letter now goes indoors. Wives and husbands first: “Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, His body, of which He is the Savior.” And the charge to husbands is not authority but the cross: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word.” His aim for her is splendor: “to present her to Himself as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish, but holy and blameless.”

The reasoning runs through a man's own body. “In the same way, husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. Indeed, no one ever hated his own body, but he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church. For we are members of His body.” Then Paul reaches back to the very first marriage and quotes Genesis: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.” His comment lifts the whole passage: “This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church.” And the summary returns it to the household: “each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband.”

Children and fathers come next, and the children get the commandment with its promise attached: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.” Then Paul quotes the commandment itself, which he notes is the first commandment with a promise: “Honor your father and mother”, “that it may go well with you and that you may have a long life on the earth.” Fathers get a restraint and a task instead: “do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.”

Then the letter speaks to the two ends of the household's hardest relationship, slaves and masters, and it speaks to both. “Slaves, obey your earthly masters with respect and fear and sincerity of heart, just as you would obey Christ,” serving “not only to please them while they are watching, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from your heart,” because “the Lord will reward each one for whatever good he does, whether he is slave or free.” And the masters are put under the same heaven: “And masters, do the same for your slaves. Give up your use of threats, because you know that He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with Him.” One Master over both chairs at the table, and no favorites in His house.

title: The Armor of God
subtitle: Ephesians 6:10–24
description: The full armor of God, prayer for an ambassador in chains, and Tychicus sent with the letter.
paragraphs: The letter's last movement opens with its own heading in Paul's voice: “Finally, be strong in the Lord and in His mighty power. Put on the full armor of God, so that you can make your stand against the devil’s schemes.” Before any piece of armor is named, the enemy is, and he is not the people across the street: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world’s darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms.”

So the order comes again, with its reason: “Therefore take up the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you will be able to stand your ground, and having done everything, to stand.” Then the pieces, in the order he gives them. “Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled around your waist, with the breastplate of righteousness arrayed, and with your feet fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace.”

Over them all, one piece is lifted up: “In addition to all this, take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” Six pieces, and only one of them is a weapon. The rest are what a soldier stands in.

And the armor is worn praying. “Pray in the Spirit at all times, with every kind of prayer and petition. To this end, stay alert with all perseverance in your prayers for all the saints.” Then the prisoner asks for himself, and what he asks for is not release: “Pray also for me, that whenever I open my mouth, words may be given me so that I will boldly make known the mystery of the gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains. Pray that I may proclaim it fearlessly, as I should.” An ambassador in chains, asking for boldness. It is the whole letter in one request.

The close names the man who carries all of this to them. “Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will tell you everything, so that you also may know about me and what I am doing. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts.” Then the last words are the letter's first words turned into a blessing over everyone who hears it: “Peace to the brothers and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with an undying love.”
